fixes.explanation: Jesus says whoever "…does not enter the sheepfold by the gate, but climbs in some other way, is a thief and a robber." (John 10:1). The gate is right there, and this guy skips it. I'd have to be one confused stamper to walk past my own front door.

Jesus never calls the climber a shepherd. He says "…the one who enters by the gate is the shepherd of the sheep." (John 10:2). The one who "…climbs in some other way, is a thief and a robber." (John 10:1). Nervous or not isn't in the picture, friend. The word Jesus uses is thief and robber.

This one is true, friend. Jesus says, "…the one who enters by the gate is the shepherd of the sheep." (John 10:2). The one who climbs in some other way is the one He calls a thief and a robber (John 10:1). So the shepherd is the one who comes in by the gate.

Jesus doesn't say anything about the youngest here. He says, "He calls his own sheep by name and leads them out." (John 10:3). The word that matters is "own." Those are the sheep he calls and leads out.

Jesus says the shepherd "…goes on ahead of them, and his sheep follow him because they know his voice." (John 10:4). He's out in front, and they come along after him. The reason Jesus gives is his voice. That's the word to hold onto.

That's backwards from what Jesus says. The shepherd "…goes on ahead of them, and his sheep follow him…" (John 10:4). The sheep are the ones following, and he's the one in front. If I stood at the back of my own cookie line, I'd be leading nobody but the crumbs.

Right, they didn't follow it. John says, "…they did not understand what He was telling them." (John 10:6). Then the very next verse says, "So He said to them again…" (John 10:7). Jesus speaks to them again.

Jesus says, "…I am the gate for the sheep." (John 10:7). Back in John 10:2 the shepherd was the one who comes in by the gate. Now Jesus says He is the gate. That's a new way of looking at the same picture.

Jesus says the opposite. About all who came before Him, He says, "…the sheep did not listen to them." (John 10:8). Those thieves and robbers had their say, and the sheep didn't listen. Not a single one of them got through to the flock.

False, friend. Jesus says those who came before Him were thieves and robbers, and then adds that the sheep did not listen to them (John 10:8). It's the same kind of moment as the stranger's voice back in John 10:5. Tough crowd, those sheep.
Jesus says, "I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved." (John 10:9). Notice the word "anyone," friend. The next sentence adds, "He will come in and go out and find pasture."
Jesus doesn't say tested. He says, "I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved." (John 10:9). That's a promise, not a test. And the verse adds that he will find pasture.
Counting never comes up in this verse. Jesus says, "I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved." (John 10:9). Saved is the word, friend. I'd take that over a clipboard any day.

Jesus says, "…I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness." (John 10:10). Right before that He says, "The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy." I think that part is heavy, so I'll just say it plain. The thief comes to take, and Jesus says He came so the sheep may have life.

Rest sounds nice, but that's not the word. Jesus says, "…I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness." (John 10:10). He's talking about something way bigger than a nap. It's life.

Shelter sounds right for a sheepfold picture, but it isn't the word. Jesus says, "…I have come that they may have life, and have it in all its fullness." (John 10:10). Life is what He says He came to give. And He says it comes in all its fullness.

Jesus says, "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep." (John 10:11). I think this one is heavy, friend, so I'll say it plain. He doesn't only guide the sheep. He lays down His own life for them.

Jesus doesn't mention counting. He says, "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep." (John 10:11). That's a much bigger thing than a nightly check. It's His own life He lays down for them.
No gate-building here. Jesus has already said He is the gate (John 10:9). About the shepherd, He says, "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep." (John 10:11).

Jesus says, "…When he sees the wolf coming, he abandons the sheep and runs away." (John 10:12). That's the hired hand, and the verse says the sheep are not his own. When the wolf comes, he leaves them. That's the difference Jesus is drawing.

Jesus says, "The man runs away because he is a hired servant and is unconcerned for the sheep." (John 10:13). The sheep aren't his own, and the verse says he is unconcerned for them. That puts him in sharp contrast with the good shepherd, who lays down His life for the sheep (John 10:11).

Jesus says, "…I know My sheep and My sheep know Me, just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father." (John 10:14-15). Let that sink in. He sets His knowing of the sheep right beside the Father and Him knowing each other. That's no casual hello at the gate.
It's true, friend. Jesus says, "…I know My sheep and My sheep know Me, just as the Father knows Me and I know the Father." (John 10:14-15). He puts the two side by side. It's a deep kind of knowing.

Jesus says He has other sheep that are not of this fold, and He must bring them in as well. When He does, He says there will be "…one flock and one shepherd." (John 10:16). That's the picture, friend. One flock, and one shepherd leading it.

Jesus doesn't leave it at two. He says He must bring in His other sheep, and then there will be "…one flock and one shepherd." (John 10:16). It isn't two flocks sharing a shepherd. They come together as one.

That's not how Jesus puts it. After He brings in His other sheep, He says there will be "…one flock and one shepherd." (John 10:16). Not two flocks standing side by side. They are one flock, with one shepherd.

Jesus says the opposite: "No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord…" (John 10:18). Nobody snatches it away from Him. He also says He has authority to lay it down and authority to take it up again. And He says He received this charge from His Father.

That's right. Jesus says, "No one takes it from Me…" (John 10:18). He lays it down of His own accord. He also says He has authority both to lay it down and to take it up again, a charge He received from His Father.

The others say, "These are not the words of a man possessed by a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?" (John 10:21). They answer the charge with a question. Opening blind eyes is the thing they point to. That's a hard question to argue with.
That's not what they point to. In John 10:21 the others say, "…Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?" Their argument is about opening blind eyes. Nothing in this verse mentions Sabbath rules.

Nobody says that here. John tells us "…there was division among the Jews because of Jesus’ message." (John 10:19). The others answer with a question, "…Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?" (John 10:21). That's what they point to.
